name: Oscar White
opening_statement: Oscar is an 18-month-old boy brought in by his mother for diarrhoea and vomiting over the past 2 days. She's concerned about dehydration.
emotional_baseline: Moderately distressed; irritable when approached but consolable by mother. Intermittently crying. Mother appears anxious about fluid intake.

symptoms.name: Diarrhoea
symptoms.progression: Gradually worsening over first 24 hours, stable since

rag_citation.reference: Gastroenteritis in children: acute watery diarrhoea typically 5-10 stools/day in viral gastroenteritis
rag_citation.relevance: Symptom frequency and character matches viral gastroenteritis pattern

symptoms.name: Vomiting
symptoms.frequency: 4-5 episodes in first 24 hours, 2 episodes today

rag_citation.reference: Acute gastroenteritis: vomiting typically precedes diarrhoea and resolves within 24-48 hours
rag_citation.relevance: Timeline matches typical viral gastroenteritis progression

symptoms.name: Decreased urine output
symptoms.frequency: Only 2 wet nappies in past 24 hours (normal 6-8)

rag_citation.reference: Dehydration assessment in children: decreased urine output (<3 wet nappies/24h in infants) indicates mild-moderate dehydration

symptoms.name: Reduced oral intake
symptoms.frequency: Refusing most feeds, taking small sips
symptoms.characteristics: Tolerating small amounts of water, refusing milk

medications.name: Paracetamol
medications.indication: Fever, given twice in past 2 days

family_history: Mother and father well. Older sibling (4 years) had similar illness last week (now recovered). No family history of chronic gastrointestinal conditions, immunodeficiency, or coeliac disease.

social_history.living_situation: Lives with both parents and 4-year-old sister in suburban home
social_history.developmental_milestones: Meeting all milestones - walking well, saying 10-15 words
social_history.diet: Normal toddler diet - breastfeeding ceased at 12 months, regular family meals
social_history.recent_contacts: Sister had gastroenteritis last week. Several children unwell at childcare.

examination_findings.general: Alert but irritable toddler, consolable by mother. Mildly lethargic when unstimulated.

hydration_status.fontanelle: Soft, not sunken (anterior fontanelle still palpable)

examination_findings.cardiovascular: Normal heart sounds, no murmurs. Peripheral pulses strong and equal.
examination_findings.respiratory: Clear breath sounds bilaterally, no increased work of breathing
examination_findings.abdominal: Soft, mildly tender diffusely on palpation, increased bowel sounds, no organomegaly, no masses
examination_findings.neurological: Alert, normal tone, age-appropriate interaction when not crying

indicated_but_not_performed: Stool microscopy/culture (not required for uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis)
Electrolytes (clinical dehydration assessment sufficient for mild dehydration)

imaging.not_indicated: No imaging required for uncomplicated gastroenteritis

expected_management.intervention: Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) - Gastrolyte/Hydralyte 5ml every 5 minutes initially
expected_management.rationale: First-line treatment for mild-moderate dehydration in gastroenteritis (eTG recommendation)
expected_management.mbs_item: None (ORT is PBS-listed for community use)
expected_management.pbs_restriction: Gastrolyte available over-the-counter, PBS-listed for community gastroenteritis management

expected_management.intervention: Demonstrate ORT technique to mother - small frequent volumes, increase as tolerated
expected_management.rationale: Parental education critical for successful home management

expected_management.intervention: Continue breastfeeding/normal feeds once vomiting settles (after 4-6 hours ORT)
expected_management.rationale: Early refeeding reduces duration of diarrhoea (eTG evidence-based)
No evidence of benefit, potential harm in children

expected_management.intervention: Red flag advice - return if: no urine for 8+ hours, blood in stool, persistent vomiting, lethargy worsening, sunken eyes/fontanelle
expected_management.rationale: Safety-netting for complications requiring IV rehydration

expected_management.intervention: Review in 24 hours if not improving, or sooner if concerns
expected_management.rationale: Monitor hydration status and ensure appropriate trajectory

expected_management.intervention: Exclude from childcare until 24 hours after last loose stool
expected_management.rationale: Infection control - reduce transmission to other children

expected_management.intervention: Hand hygiene education for family members
expected_management.rationale: Reduce household transmission (viral gastroenteritis highly contagious)

critical_errors.error: Prescribing IV fluids without attempting oral rehydration therapy first
critical_errors.justification: ORT is first-line for mild-moderate dehydration per eTG guidelines. IV therapy exposes child to unnecessary procedural risks and should be reserved for severe dehydration or ORT failure.

critical_errors.error: Prescribing loperamide or other anti-motility agents
critical_errors.justification: Contraindicated in children <12 years due to risk of ileus, toxic megacolon. No evidence of benefit in viral gastroenteritis.

critical_errors.error: Prescribing antibiotics for uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis
critical_errors.justification: Viral aetiology most likely (no blood/mucus in stool, contact history). Antibiotics inappropriate without evidence of bacterial infection, promote resistance.

critical_errors.error: Advising to withhold all feeds until diarrhoea stops
critical_errors.justification: Early refeeding (after initial ORT) reduces duration of diarrhoea. Prolonged fasting increases risk of malnutrition in young children.

critical_errors.error: Failing to provide safety-netting advice about red flags for deterioration
critical_errors.justification: Parents must know when to return urgently (e.g., persistent vomiting preventing ORT, signs of severe dehydration). Omission risks delayed recognition of complications.

critical_errors.error: Not assessing hydration status systematically (mucous membranes, tears, urine output, skin turgor)
critical_errors.justification: Incomplete assessment may miss severity of dehydration. However, if ORT advised appropriately, outcome may still be acceptable.

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FRACP (Paediatrics), Staff Specialist, Sydney Children's Hospital
fracp_reviews.clinical_accuracy: Excellent representation of typical viral gastroenteritis in toddler. Mild dehydration features appropriate for 'Easy' difficulty. Contact history (sibling, childcare) realistic.
fracp_reviews.difficulty_appropriateness: Correctly calibrated as Easy - straightforward diagnosis, single system involvement, no comorbidities, uncomplicated management with ORT.
fracp_reviews.learning_value: High-yield scenario for AMC Clinical Exam. Tests core paediatric skills: hydration assessment, ORT technique, safety-netting, infection control advice.
fracp_reviews.suggested_improvements: None - scenario is appropriate for target difficulty level.

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FRACP (Paediatrics & Child Health), Director of Paediatric Emergency, Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne
fracp_reviews.clinical_accuracy: Clinically accurate. Symptom progression (vomiting settling before diarrhoea), viral epidemiology (childcare exposure), and mild dehydration signs all consistent with common presentation.
fracp_reviews.difficulty_appropriateness: Appropriate for Easy level. Single diagnosis, no diagnostic uncertainty, standard first-line management. No red herrings or atypical features.
fracp_reviews.learning_value: Essential bread-and-butter paediatrics. Critical errors appropriately focus on guideline-based practice (ORT first-line, avoid anti-motility drugs). Tests communication skills for parental education.
fracp_reviews.suggested_improvements: Consider adding specific volume of ORT to prescribe (e.g., '50ml/kg over 4 hours for deficit replacement') for advanced learners, but not essential for Easy level.

learning_objectives: Perform systematic hydration assessment in young children using clinical signs (mucous membranes, tears, urine output, capillary refill, skin turgor, fontanelle)
Differentiate mild, moderate, and severe dehydration based on clinical criteria (WHO/eTG guidelines)
Apply oral rehydration therapy as first-line treatment for mild-moderate dehydration (5ml every 5 minutes technique)
Counsel parents on red flag symptoms requiring urgent re-assessment (persistent vomiting, no urine 8+ hours, lethargy, bloody stool)
Understand contraindications to anti-diarrhoeal medications in paediatric gastroenteritis (loperamide <12 years)
Implement infection control measures for viral gastroenteritis (exclusion from childcare, hand hygiene)
Apply early refeeding principles to reduce illness duration (continue age-appropriate diet after initial ORT phase)
Distinguish viral from bacterial gastroenteritis using clinical features (contact history, stool character, absence of systemic toxicity)
